newsitem.title: USA: Ex Clinton aide's wife says hurt by husband's affair.
newsitem.headline: Ex Clinton aide's wife says hurt by husband's affair.

text.p: - The wife of political consultant Dick Morris said in an interview published Sunday she is not blindly supporting her husband after his affair with a prostitute and their relationship is "day to day."
"I never said I'm standing by this man no matter what," Eileen McGann told Newsweek magazine. "I don't know where I'm going to be six months or a year from now."
"I'm taking it day by day," she said. "I know one thing: I'm not going to leave someone who's been my best friend for 20 years."

Morris quit as one of President Clinton's top political advisers after a supermarket tabloid reported he had an affair with a $200-an-hour prostitute for nearly a year and let her listen in on phone calls with the White House.
Since then, McGann, a trial lawyer, has been seen standing by his side, providing support.

"While I'm trying very hard to understand, that doesn't mean I don't feel any pain or anger," she said. "I'm not happy about what he did, and sometimes I think about dismembering him, and good friends have offered to help me dig up the backyard and bury him."

After quitting the Clinton campaign, Morris signed a $2.5 million book deal. In a poll accompanying the interview, Newsweek reported that 39 percent of those questioned said they believed McGann was staying with Morris for financial gain. Thirty-six percent said she was doing so because she is understanding.

McGann said, "There are easier ways to make money than being dragged through something like this in public for weeks and weeks. I'm financially self-sufficient. That's not what motivates me. What's motivating me is a deep concern for someone I've been close to and who has been deeply supportive of me for 20 years."
She said Morris spends his days writing and "is suffering terribly."

The Newsweek poll dealt with the public's view of adultery. It also showed that 76 percent of the 751 adults questioned believe extra-marital affairs are always wrong but 51 percent think they are more common now than 10 years ago.
